Plain_Summary: Covered employees of frontier developers are protected when they disclose information about catastrophic risk or a violation of SB 53: a developer may not make, adopt, enforce or enter into any rule, policy or contract that prevents such disclosure or retaliates for it, may not contractually bar a disclosure protected under Lab. Code §1102.5, and must let covered employees use the §1102.7 hotline. Every frontier developer must give notice of these rights by continuous workplace posting (with equivalent notice to new and remote employees) or by annual written notice with receipt acknowledged. Large frontier developers must also run a reasonable anonymous internal process for such disclosures, give the discloser monthly status updates, and share disclosures and responses quarterly with officers and directors (except an implicated officer or director). Remedies include attorney's fees, burden-shifting and injunctive relief.
Applies_To: All frontier developers for (a)-(d); large frontier developers only for (e). Covered employees are employees responsible for assessing, managing or addressing critical-safety-incident risk.
Notes: Verified via the public.law verbatim mirror, cross-checked against the Greenberg Traurig alert, the Assembly Privacy Committee analysis (11 Sep 2025) and oag.ca.gov/sb53; a direct leginfo read of the Lab. Code chapter is still outstanding (U-02). Lab. Code §1107(c)(1) defines critical safety incident more broadly than Bus. & Prof. Code §22757.11(d)(1): it also covers property damage or loss. Contractors are not covered employees; the Assembly analysis records that contractors were removed from the definition. Lab. Code §1107.2 content is substantively answered (Justia full text, 21 Nov 2026: a single interpretive sentence — loss of equity value does not count as damage to or loss of property; no developer duty) but the official SEC. 4 / codified read is still outstanding (U-01); no row is added for it. No duty in this row falls on a deployer.

Plain_Summary: Definitions and thresholds that set the scope of the duties in §§22757.12-22757.13 and 22757.15. A frontier model is a foundation model trained with more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, counting the original run plus later fine-tuning, reinforcement learning or other material modifications. A frontier developer is a person who trained or initiated training of such a model. A large frontier developer is a frontier developer that, together with its affiliates, collectively had annual gross revenues above $500M in the preceding calendar year. Catastrophic risk is a foreseeable, material risk of death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1B property damage or loss, from a single incident, via three mechanisms (assistance with weapons of mass destruction, unsupervised cyberattack or violent-crime conduct, evading control), subject to stated exclusions. A critical safety incident covers weight theft or access causing death or bodily injury, harm from a materialised catastrophic risk, loss of control causing death or bodily injury, and deceptive subversion of controls outside an evaluation showing materially increased catastrophic risk.
Applies_To: Frontier developers and large frontier developers (definitions set the scope of the duties in §§22757.12-22757.13 and 22757.15; this section imposes no duty by itself)
Notes: Definitions only; imposes no duty by itself. §22757.11(d)(1) requires death or bodily injury from weight theft or access, while the Lab. Code §1107(c)(1) whistleblower definition is broader (it also covers property damage or loss) — whether that divergence is intentional is an attorney question (Pass 1).

Plain_Summary: Large frontier developers must write, implement, comply with and clearly and conspicuously publish on their website a frontier AI framework describing how they approach catastrophic-risk assessment and mitigation, covering ten topics (national and international standards and industry best practices; risk thresholds; mitigations; deploy-decision review; third-party assessment; framework updates; cybersecurity for unreleased model weights; incident response; internal governance; internal-use risk). They must review and update the framework at least once per year and publish material modifications with justification within 30 days. Before or concurrently with deploying a new or substantially modified frontier model, every frontier developer must publish a transparency report (developer website; a mechanism enabling a natural person to communicate with the developer; release date; languages; output modalities; intended uses; use restrictions). Large developers must add summaries of catastrophic-risk assessments, results, third-party involvement and other framework steps. A system or model card carrying the same information counts as compliance.
Applies_To: Large frontier developers for the framework (a)-(b) and the (c)(2) assessment summaries; ALL frontier developers for the (c)(1) transparency report. Large means collective annual gross revenues of the developer together with its affiliates in excess of $500M in the preceding calendar year; frontier models are trained with more than 10^26 operations.
Notes: The (d) quarterly internal-use summaries, (e) false-statement ban and (f) redactions and 5-year retention are separate rows (CA-SB53-22757-12D and CA-SB53-22757-12EF). Framework topic (a)(7), cybersecurity practices to secure unreleased model weights, has no ISO 42001 counterpart in this module and is unmapped. The (c)(1)(B) contact mechanism is mapped at A.8.3. No duty in this row falls on a deployer.

Plain_Summary: Large frontier developers must transmit to the California Office of Emergency Services a summary of catastrophic-risk assessments from internal use of frontier models every three months, or on another reasonable schedule communicated in writing. CalOES must keep these summaries in a confidential channel with need-to-know access limits under §22757.13(b).
Applies_To: Large frontier developers (collective annual gross revenues of the developer together with its affiliates in excess of $500M in the preceding calendar year; frontier models trained with more than 10^26 operations)
Notes: The CalOES TFAIA reporting page (read 2026-11-21) links a secure portal accepting these summaries; the portal itself was not opened (U-03); portal URL identified in Fix Pass 2 — https://app.kaseware.us/public/#CALOES/e8921920-9735-4798-b24d-9c28c306f6e8 — open in a live browser and confirm both submission paths accept filings. These summaries are confidential transmittals to CalOES, not public documentation. No duty in this row falls on a deployer.

Plain_Summary: No frontier developer may make a materially false or misleading statement about catastrophic risk; large frontier developers likewise may not make such statements about implementing or complying with their frontier AI framework. Statements made in good faith and reasonably are excepted. A developer may redact material from a published framework or transparency report on trade-secret, cybersecurity, public-safety, national-security or legal-compliance grounds, stating the character of the redaction and its justification, and must retain the unredacted material for five years.
Applies_To: All frontier developers for catastrophic-risk statements under (e); large frontier developers for framework implementation and compliance statements under (e) and for (f)
Notes: A false statement under (e) carries penalty exposure under §22757.15 (see CA-SB53-22757-15). No duty in this row falls on a deployer.

Plain_Summary: Frontier developers must report a critical safety incident to the California Office of Emergency Services within 15 days of discovering it, and disclose an incident to an appropriate authority (including law enforcement or a public safety agency with jurisdiction) within 24 hours where there is imminent risk of death or serious physical injury, as required by law.
Applies_To: Frontier developers (all frontier developers, not only large ones)
Notes: Amended reports are allowed on new information (c)(3); reporting is encouraged, not required, for non-frontier foundation models (c)(4). CalOES produces its first annual anonymized, aggregated incident report to the Legislature and Governor on 1 Jan 2027 (g). Under (h)-(i) CalOES may designate federal law or guidance as substantially equivalent or stricter, and a developer declaring intent to comply via it is deemed compliant to that extent; no CalOES designation was found as of 2026-11-21, re-check quarterly (Pass 1 SB53-U7). The CalOES reporting mechanism is operable per the CalOES TFAIA page read 2026-11-21; the portal itself was not opened. No duty in this row falls on a deployer.

Plain_Summary: A large frontier developer that fails to publish or transmit a required compliant document, makes a false statement banned by §22757.12(e), fails to report under §22757.13, or fails to comply with its own frontier AI framework is subject to a civil penalty scaled to severity, capped at $1M per violation. The penalty is recoverable only in a civil action brought by the Attorney General; there is no private right of action under the chapter.
Applies_To: Large frontier developers (collective annual gross revenues of the developer together with its affiliates in excess of $500M in the preceding calendar year; frontier models trained with more than 10^26 operations)
Notes: No AG enforcement action under this section was found as of 2026-11-21 (Pass 1 SB53-U8); re-check the AG press releases and SB 53 page at each quarterly review. This section imposes no substantive duty of its own; it is the enforcement consequence for the duties in §§22757.12-22757.13.

Plain_Summary: Developers of generative AI systems made publicly available to Californians must publish on their website a high-level summary of the training datasets covering at least 12 items: dataset sources or owners; how the datasets further the system's intended purpose; data-point counts in general ranges; types of data points; whether datasets include intellectual-property-protected data or are entirely public domain; whether purchased or licensed; whether they include personal information or aggregate consumer information; whether the datasets were cleaned, processed or otherwise modified and the intended purpose; the collection time period; the dates datasets were first used; and whether synthetic-data generation was used, before public availability or a substantial modification.
Applies_To: Developers of generative AI systems made publicly available to Californians
Notes: Statute effective 1 Jan 2025 (Ch. 817, Stats. 2024); §3111 itself requires the first posting on or before 1 Jan 2026, and again before each later public release or substantial modification of a system released on or after 1 Jan 2022. §3111 as amended by AB 1170 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 67, Sec. 35), nonsubstantive, effective 1 Jan 2026. Exempt per §3111(b): systems whose sole purpose is ensuring security and integrity; systems whose sole purpose is operating aircraft in the national airspace; and national security, military or defense systems made available only to a federal entity. Litigation: X.AI v. Bonta, preliminary injunction denied 4 Mar 2026, 9th Cir. No. 26-1591 argued 18 Nov 2026 with no decision as of 21 Nov 2026; the statute remains in force. The statute names no enforcer or penalty.

Plain_Summary: A business must carry out and document a risk assessment before starting processing that presents significant risk to consumers' privacy. Six triggers are listed in section 7150(b), including selling or sharing personal information, processing sensitive personal information, using automated decision-making technology for a significant decision, automated profiling inferences about applicants, students, employees or contractors, inferences from presence in a sensitive location, and processing personal information the business intends to use to train automated decision-making technology for a significant decision or to train facial-recognition, emotion-recognition or other identity-verification technology.
Applies_To: CCPA-covered businesses
Notes: Assessment required before initiation of new processing from 1 Jan 2026 (section 7155(a)(1)); processing begun before 1 Jan 2026 and continuing after it must be assessed by 31 Dec 2027 (section 7155(b)). A significant decision (section 7001(ddd)) is one resulting in provision or denial of financial or lending services, housing, education enrollment or opportunities, employment or independent-contracting opportunities or compensation, or healthcare services; advertising to a consumer is expressly excluded. Covered business means a for-profit entity doing business in California that determines the purposes and means of processing and meets one of the Civil Code section 1798.140(d) tests, including annual gross revenue above the inflation-adjusted $26,625,000 threshold. Regulations adopted 24 Jul 2025, approved by the Office of Administrative Law 22 Sep 2025, effective 1 Jan 2026.

Plain_Summary: The risk assessment must be recorded in a documented, approved report covering the specific purpose, the personal information categories involved, the operational elements of the processing, the benefits, the negative privacy impacts with their sources and causes, the safeguards applied, whether the business will initiate the processing, the information providers, and the review and approval date with the reviewers and approvers. The automated decision-making technology logic, assumptions, limitations and output are required only for assessments of technology used for a significant decision under section 7150(b)(3).
Applies_To: CCPA-covered businesses
Notes: Assessment required before initiation from 1 Jan 2026 (section 7155(a)(1)); pre-2026 processing backfilled by 31 Dec 2027 (section 7155(b)). Review and update at least every three years and within 45 calendar days of a material change (section 7155(a)(2)-(3)); retain assessments for as long as processing continues or five years after completion, whichever is later (section 7155(c)). Employees whose duties include participating in the processing must be included in the assessment process (section 7151); one assessment may cover a comparable set of similar processing activities, and an assessment prepared for another purpose may be reused if it contains or is paired with the section 7152 information (section 7156).

Plain_Summary: A business that makes automated decision-making technology available to another business for that business to use in making a significant decision must give the recipient business all facts available to it that the recipient needs to conduct its own risk assessment. The duty applies only to technology trained using personal information.
Applies_To: CCPA-covered businesses making ADMT available to another business for a significant decision
Notes: New row in Pass 2 (Pass 0 major, provider-deployer gap). The only provider-to-recipient duty in the package: the supplying business is the facts provider and the recipient business carries out its own assessment; the supplying business is not required to assess the recipient's processing itself. Operative from the regulations' 1 Jan 2026 effective date.

Plain_Summary: A business must submit risk-assessment information to the California Privacy Protection Agency, including the number of assessments conducted or updated and an attestation by an executive-management member that the business conducted the assessments and that the submitter meets the section's requirements, made under penalty of perjury. For assessments conducted in 2026 and 2027 the submission is due by 1 Apr 2028; for later years it is due by 1 Apr after the year of the assessments. The Agency or the Attorney General may also require the full risk-assessment reports at any time, and the business must produce them within 30 calendar days.
Applies_To: CCPA-covered businesses that conducted §7150(b) risk assessments
Notes: New row in Pass 2 (Pass 0 blocker). First submission deadline 1 Apr 2028 for 2026-2027 assessments (section 7157(a)(1)); annual thereafter (section 7157(a)(2)); full reports within 30 calendar days on Agency or Attorney General demand (section 7157(e)). Submitter must be an executive-management member directly responsible for risk-assessment compliance, with sufficient knowledge and authority to submit (section 7157(c)); submission via the Agency website (section 7157(d)). The live submission portal or form was not confirmed in Pass 1 (U-06); check the Agency website before the 1 Apr 2028 deadline.

Plain_Summary: A business whose processing of consumers' personal information presents significant risk to consumers' security must complete an annual cybersecurity audit assessing how its cybersecurity program protects personal information and whether the program is established, implemented and maintained, including each applicable component listed in section 7123(c). The audit must be carried out by a qualified, objective and independent professional, its findings must rest on specific evidence rather than primarily on management assertions, and the report must identify gaps, set out a remediation plan with timeframes, and be delivered to an executive with direct cybersecurity-program responsibility.
Applies_To: CCPA-covered businesses meeting the significant-security-risk test in §7120(b)
Notes: New row in Pass 2 (Pass 0 major, missing duty). Significant-risk test (section 7120(b)): the business derived 50 percent or more of revenue from selling or sharing personal information in the preceding year, or met the revenue threshold and processed personal information of 250,000 or more consumers or households, or sensitive personal information of 50,000 or more consumers. First reports due 1 Apr 2028 (revenue over $100M, period 1 Jan 2027-1 Jan 2028), 1 Apr 2029 ($50M-$100M), 1 Apr 2030 (under $50M); annual thereafter, report by 1 Apr of the following year (section 7121). Audit records retained at least five years (section 7122). Split from the section 7124 certification, which is a separate filing duty, into its own row (CA-CCPA-CYBER-7124).

Plain_Summary: Each year a cybersecurity audit is required, the business must submit a written certification of completion to the Agency, including the business name and point of contact, a statement that the audit was completed, the period covered, and an electronically signed attestation under penalty of perjury by an executive-management member directly responsible for audit compliance.
Applies_To: CCPA-covered businesses meeting the significant-security-risk test in §7120(b)
Notes: New row in Pass 2, split from CA-CCPA-CYBER-7120 (Pass 0 major): the audit itself (sections 7120-7123) and the annual certification of completion (section 7124) are distinct duties with different actors and deadlines, so they are separate rows. Due no later than 1 Apr following each audit year; submission via the Agency website. The live certification portal or form was not confirmed in Pass 1 (U-06).

Plain_Summary: A business that uses automated decision-making technology to make a significant decision about a consumer must comply with Article 11. Uses already underway before 1 Jan 2027 must comply no later than 1 Jan 2027; uses starting on or after 1 Jan 2027 must comply whenever the technology is used for a significant decision. Section 7200 sets applicability and timing only; the pre-use notice, opt-out and access duties themselves are in sections 7220-7222.
Applies_To: CCPA-covered businesses using ADMT for a significant decision
Notes: Re-scoped in Pass 2 (Pass 0 major, citation-scope error): the base row described sections 7220-7222 content under a section 7200 citation. Effective date corrected from 2026-01-01 to 2027-01-01 (section 7200(b)); the regulations as a whole are in force from 1 Jan 2026. A significant decision (section 7001(ddd)) covers provision or denial of financial or lending services, housing, education enrollment or opportunities, employment or independent-contracting opportunities or compensation, or healthcare services; advertising is expressly excluded. See CA-ADMT-7220, CA-ADMT-7221 and CA-ADMT-7222 for the notice, opt-out and access duties.

Plain_Summary: Before automated decision-making technology is used for a significant decision, the business must give the consumer a pre-use notice at or before collecting the personal information to be processed (or before processing if it was already collected for another purpose), explaining the specific purpose, the consumer's opt-out and access rights, how the technology works, what output it produces and how it is used, and the alternative process for consumers who opt out. Where an opt-out exception is relied on, the notice must instead describe the human appeal or name the exception. Trade secrets and certain security information need not be disclosed.
Applies_To: CCPA-covered businesses using ADMT for a significant decision
Notes: Effective date corrected from 2026-01-01 to 2027-01-01 (section 7200(b)): pre-2027 uses must comply no later than 1 Jan 2027; uses on or after 1 Jan 2027 must comply at time of use. Significant decision per section 7001(ddd); advertising excluded. Sub-paragraph detail in sections 7220(b)-(e) re-read in full from the official text and confirmed (Fix Pass 2, 21 Nov 2026).

Plain_Summary: A consumer may opt out of automated decision-making technology being used for a significant decision about them. No opt-out is required where the business offers a qualifying human appeal, where the technology is used solely to assess ability to perform for admission, acceptance or hiring decisions and works for that purpose without unlawfully discriminating, or for work-allocation or compensation decisions on the same sole-purpose conditions. The business must offer two or more submission methods, at least one reflecting the primary interaction channel, must not require an account or a verifiable consumer request, and must confirm the opt-out was processed. If the opt-out arrives before processing, the business must not initiate it; if after processing began, it must stop as soon as feasibly possible and no later than 15 business days.
Applies_To: CCPA-covered businesses using ADMT for a significant decision
Notes: New row in Pass 2 (Pass 0 major, missing duty). Operative 1 Jan 2027 (section 7200(b)). Where an exception is relied on, the pre-use notice must describe the appeal or name the exception (see CA-ADMT-7220). 12-month wait verified in the official text, section 7221(k) (Fix Pass 2, 21 Nov 2026): except as allowed by the regulations, a business must wait at least 12 months from receipt of the opt-out request before asking the consumer to consent again to the ADMT use previously opted out of.

Plain_Summary: On request, a business that used automated decision-making technology for a significant decision about a consumer must give a plain-language explanation of the specific purpose, the technology's logic including how it processed the consumer's personal information, the outcome including how the output was used and the human role, and non-retaliation and how to use other rights. Service providers and contractors must assist the business with access requests, including by returning or enabling access to relevant consumer data.
Applies_To: CCPA-covered businesses using ADMT for a significant decision
Notes: New row in Pass 2 (Pass 0 major, missing duty). Operative 1 Jan 2027 (section 7200(b)). Timing follows the Article 5 request rules (acknowledgement within 10 business days; response within 45 calendar days, one 45-day extension with notice; denial if the consumer cannot be verified). Timing and aggregate-response rule verified in the official text (Fix Pass 2, 21 Nov 2026): timing per Article 5, section 7021 (acknowledgement within 10 business days; response within 45 calendar days, one 45-day extension with notice, 90-day maximum); aggregate response per section 7222(j) where the same ADMT was used more than four times in 12 months, limited to the section 7222(b)(2) logic information.

Citation: SB 942 (Ch. 291, Stats. 2024), Bus. & Prof. Code §22757.3, as amended by AB 853 (Ch. 674, Stats. 2025) and SB 1000 (Ch. 861, Stats. 2026)
Plain_Summary: A covered provider of a generative AI system must, to the extent technically feasible, include a latent disclosure in any image, video or audio content (or a combination) that its system created or altered, except where the change is only a minor modification. The disclosure must state the provider name, the system name and version, the time and date of creation or alteration, a unique identifier, whether the system created or altered the content and, on and after 1 Jan 2029, whether the system is designed to primarily function as assistive technology; it must be permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove or tamper with, compatible with the provider's disclosure verification tool, and compliant or interoperable with widely recognized industry standards. A provider licensing its system must notify the licensee of the licensee's duties under the chapter when granting the license, and if it knows an identifiable licensee modified the system so it no longer complies, it must within 72 hours of discovery either end the licensee's authorization or notify the licensee of the noncompliance. A notified licensee must modify the system to comply or stop using or making it available, and report which action it took to the provider within 96 hours of receiving the notice; if no report arrives, or the report shows the licensee did neither, the provider must report the noncompliance to the Attorney General. The provider has no duty to monitor, investigate or inquire into licensee use or modification, and must not falsely represent a system as designed to primarily function as assistive technology.
Applies_To: Covered providers of generative AI systems and their licensees
Notes: As amended by AB 853 (Ch. 674, Stats. 2025) and SB 1000 (Ch. 861, Stats. 2026, urgency, signed 30 Sep 2026). SB 1000 removed the 1,000,000-monthly-user threshold from the covered-provider definition and deleted the manifest (visible) disclosure option; the latent disclosure now covers content created or altered. AB 2713 (Ch. 856, Stats. 2026) amended §22757.3.1 (large online platforms) only and did not touch this section. The chapter does not apply to a system designed to primarily function as assistive technology before 1 Jan 2029 (§22757.5(b)). Penalties and enforcement: $5,000 per violation under §22757.4, with each day in violation a discrete violation for a covered provider, a large online platform or a capture device manufacturer (hosting platforms and licensees are not named in the per-day rule); enforced by the Attorney General, a city attorney or a county counsel, with reasonable attorney's costs and fees to the prevailing plaintiff; no private right of action. A false assistive-technology representation under §22757.3(d) is penalized separately at $50,000 per violation under §22757.4.1, repealed 1 Jan 2029 - see also CA-SB942-22757-4-1. The Attorney General must establish a mechanism to receive provider reports (§22757.3(c)); whether that mechanism exists is UNVERIFIED (U-08; no mechanism found in Fix Pass 2 searches of oag.ca.gov, 21 Nov 2026). Codified display not directly verified (leginfo returned HTTP 403 on 2026-11-21); verified against the SB 1000 chaptered text - see U-07 (live-browser check outstanding).

Citation: SB 942 (Ch. 291, Stats. 2024), Bus. & Prof. Code §22757.2, as amended by SB 1000 (Ch. 861, Stats. 2026)
Plain_Summary: A covered provider of a generative AI system must provide a free disclosure verification tool that lets a user assess whether image, video or audio content (or a combination) was created or altered, except by minor modification, by the provider's system. The tool must output any system provenance data detected in the content and no personal information detected in it, except where the person concerned expressly consents in clear, conspicuous plain language under a notice explaining what personal information may be output and that such information embedded in provenance data and exported becomes part of the file's permanent digital footprint and cannot be retracted from copies already in circulation. The tool must be publicly accessible, subject to reasonable limits to prevent or respond to demonstrable security or integrity risks or misuse for malicious purposes; it must accept an upload or a URL, and support use without visiting the provider's website, including through an API. The provider must collect user feedback on the tool's efficacy and use relevant feedback in improvement attempts; must not collect, use, retain, sell, share or otherwise make available personal information from a tool user or from content processed by the tool beyond what is strictly necessary to comply with the chapter, except to communicate with a user who opts into being contacted; and must not condition access to its system or the tool on the user providing personal information beyond what is strictly necessary to comply. A provider may instead direct the user to a compliant third-party tool that is compatible with its latent disclosures and clearly and conspicuously accessible through the system's user interface.
Applies_To: Covered providers of generative AI systems
Notes: SB 1000 (Ch. 861, Stats. 2026) renamed the tool from 'AI detection tool' to 'disclosure verification tool'. Enforcement: $5,000 per violation under §22757.4, with each day in violation a discrete violation for a covered provider; enforced by the Attorney General, a city attorney or a county counsel; no private right of action. Codified display of §22757.2 not directly verified (leginfo returned HTTP 403 on 2026-11-21); verified against the SB 1000 chaptered text and its verbatim enrolled-text mirror - UNVERIFIED Pass 1 #1.

Citation: SB 942 (Ch. 291, Stats. 2024), Bus. & Prof. Code §22757.3.1, as added by AB 853 (Ch. 674, Stats. 2025) and rewritten by AB 2713 (Ch. 856, Stats. 2026)
Plain_Summary: A large online platform must detect whether any provenance data is embedded in, attached to or otherwise associated with content distributed on the platform, and provide a user interface that reliably indicates whether any system provenance data or digital signature in that content identifies it as generated or substantially altered by a generative AI system or captured by a capture device. The interface must make clearly and conspicuously available information sufficient to identify the content's authenticity, origin or history of modification, including whether provenance data is present and whether digital signatures are present, and the name of the generative AI system or capture device where applicable. A user must be able to inspect any system provenance data in the content in an easily accessible way - displayed through the interface, via a link to a site or application displaying it, or by downloading the data in a format that cannot easily be attached to unrelated content. The platform has no duty to maintain, display or allow download of personal information, and must not, to the extent technically feasible, knowingly strip any system provenance data or digital signature from content uploaded to, distributed on or downloaded from the platform. No action is required on provenance data, system provenance data or digital signatures that are not compliant or interoperable with widely adopted specifications issued by an established standards-setting body.
Applies_To: Large online platforms (public-facing social media, file-sharing or mass messaging platforms, or stand-alone search engines, distributing content to users who did not create or collaborate in creating it, with more than 2,000,000 unique monthly users during the preceding 12 months)
Notes: AB 2713 (Ch. 856, Stats. 2026, signed 30 Sep 2026) rewrote this section only: detection now covers any provenance data; the interface duty turns on system provenance data or a digital signature; inspection covers any system provenance data via interface, link or download; a personal-information carve-out was added; the no-strip rule was extended to downloads; and no duty applies to non-standards-compliant data. Enforcement: $5,000 per violation under §22757.4, with each day in violation a discrete violation for a large online platform; enforced by the Attorney General, a city attorney or a county counsel; no private right of action. UNVERIFIED: codified display not directly verified (leginfo HTTP 403, 2026-11-21); exact wording of §22757.3.1(a)(2)(B)(ii) not fully captured in the leginfo crawl - Pass 1 #1 and #2.

Citation: SB 942 (Ch. 291, Stats. 2024), Bus. & Prof. Code §22757.3.2, as added by AB 853 (Ch. 674, Stats. 2025)
Plain_Summary: A generative AI hosting platform must not knowingly make available a generative AI system that does not place the latent disclosures required by §22757.3.
Applies_To: GenAI hosting platforms (sites or applications making available for download the source code or model weights of a generative AI system, with or without compensation)
Notes: Single-duty section; AB 2713 did not amend it. Enforcement: $5,000 per violation under §22757.4, enforced by the Attorney General, a city attorney or a county counsel; no private right of action. Hosting platforms are not named in the §22757.4 per-day rule, so each day in violation is not automatically a discrete violation for a hosting platform. Codified display not directly verified (leginfo HTTP 403, 2026-11-21); verified against the AB 853 chaptered text - UNVERIFIED Pass 1 #1.

Citation: SB 942 (Ch. 291, Stats. 2024), Bus. & Prof. Code §22757.3.3, as added by AB 853 (Ch. 674, Stats. 2025)
Plain_Summary: For any capture device first produced for sale in California on or after 1 Jan 2028, the manufacturer must give the user the option to include a latent disclosure in captured content conveying the manufacturer name, the device name and version number, and the time and date of creation or alteration, and must embed latent disclosures in captured content by default. Compliance is required only to the extent technically feasible and compliant with widely adopted specifications adopted by an established standards-setting body.
Applies_To: Capture device manufacturers (persons producing devices that record photographs, audio or video for sale in California, excluding persons exclusively engaged in assembly)
Notes: AB 2713 did not amend this section. Enforcement: $5,000 per violation under §22757.4, with each day in violation a discrete violation for a capture device manufacturer; enforced by the Attorney General, a city attorney or a county counsel; no private right of action. Codified display not directly verified (leginfo HTTP 403, 2026-11-21); verified against the AB 853 chaptered text - UNVERIFIED Pass 1 #1.

Citation: SB 942 (Ch. 291, Stats. 2024), Bus. & Prof. Code §22757.4.1, as added by SB 1000 (Ch. 861, Stats. 2026)
Plain_Summary: A covered provider that falsely represents a generative AI system as designed to primarily function as assistive technology - the conduct banned by §22757.3(d) - faces a civil penalty of $50,000 per violation, with each day in violation a discrete violation, collected in a civil action by the Attorney General, a city attorney or a county counsel, with reasonable attorney's costs and fees to the prevailing plaintiff. This section is in effect until 1 Jan 2029 and is then repealed.
Applies_To: Covered providers of generative AI systems
Notes: §22757.4 (the $5,000 general penalty) does not apply to a §22757.3(d) violation; such violations are penalized under this section instead. The 1 Jan 2029 repeal coincides with the date the assistive-technology disclosure field in §22757.3(a)(1)(F) starts to apply and the §22757.5(b) exemption for assistive-technology systems lifts. Plain_Summary: Section 11008 sets out the general definitions used across the employment regulations, including agent, applicant, employee, employer and proxy. A person acting as the employer's agent, including by administering an automated-decision system on the employer's behalf, also counts as an employer for Fair Employment and Housing Act purposes (section 11008(b) and (f)(3)). The employer definition covers employers regularly employing five or more people, counting part-time and out-of-state employees, plus the State and political subdivisions regardless of size, and excludes non-profit religious organisations (section 11008(f)).
Applies_To: California employers regularly employing 5 or more people, including employers using automated-decision systems in employment decisions; the State and political subdivisions regardless of size; non-profit religious organisations excluded
Notes: Definitions section only; it imposes no duty to assess or test an automated-decision system. The automated-decision system definition itself is section 11008.1 — see CA-FEHA-11008-1. Adopted text relettered section 11008 (new (a) Reserved); Agent is section 11008(b) and Employer is section 11008(f).

Plain_Summary: Section 11008.1 defines an automated-decision system as a computational process, including one using artificial intelligence, machine learning or other algorithmic techniques, that makes a decision about an employment benefit or facilitates a human decision about one. In-scope tasks include computer-based assessments and tests, directing job advertisements to targeted groups, screening resumes for terms or patterns, analysing facial expression, word choice or voice in online interviews, and analysing third-party applicant or employee data. Excluded are ordinary tools such as word processing, spreadsheets, maps, web hosting, data storage, firewalls, spam filtering, spellchecking, calculators and databases, provided they do not decide an employment benefit. Automated-decision system data (section 11008.1(d)) covers data used in or resulting from the system, plus data used to develop or customise it for a particular employer.
Applies_To: California employers regularly employing 5 or more people, including employers using automated-decision systems in employment decisions; the State and political subdivisions regardless of size; non-profit religious organisations excluded
Notes: The defined term 'automated-decision system data' is the term the section 11013 retention duty turns on — see CA-FEHA-11013. The regulations impose no standalone duty to tell an applicant or employee that an automated-decision system is in use.

Plain_Summary: Section 11009(f) makes it unlawful to use an automated-decision system or other selection criteria, including a qualification standard, employment test or proxy, that discriminates on a protected basis, subject to any available defence. Evidence, or the lack of it, of anti-bias testing or similar proactive efforts is relevant to a discrimination claim, including the quality, efficacy, recency and scope of the effort, its results, and the response to the results.
Theme: Non-discrimination prohibition and anti-bias testing evidence
Applies_To: California employers regularly employing 5 or more people, including employers using automated-decision systems in employment decisions; the State and political subdivisions regardless of size; non-profit religious organisations excluded
Notes: Evidentiary factor in discrimination claims, not a freestanding duty to conduct anti-bias testing. Basis-specific automated-decision system insertions in 2 CCR sections 11028, 11032, 11033, 11038, 11039, 11056, 11063, 11070, 11071, 11076 and 11079 repeat the section 11009(f) prohibition formula and are not separately rowed, except section 11072 item (F) — see CA-FEHA-11072.

Plain_Summary: Employers must preserve personnel and employment records, expressly including selection criteria and automated-decision system data, for at least four years from the later of the record date or the personnel action. Once a complaint is filed, relevant records, expressly including automated-decision system data, must be preserved until the later of the expiry of the civil-action filing period or the full and final disposition of the complaint and all related proceedings, so the hold can run longer than four years.
Applies_To: California employers regularly employing 5 or more people, including employers using automated-decision systems in employment decisions; the State and political subdivisions regardless of size; non-profit religious organisations excluded
Notes: Row scoped to section 11013(c) record preservation. The California Employer Information Report under section 11013(a) applies only to employers regularly employing 100 or more people (plus apprenticeship and labour-organisation thresholds); applicant identification records carry their own four-year rule under section 11013(b) and (c)(2).

Plain_Summary: Section 11016(a)(2) bars recruitment through an automated-decision system that restricts, excludes or classifies applicants on a protected basis, expresses a preference on that basis, or uses discriminatory advertising. Section 11016(b)(1) bars pre-employment inquiries made through an automated-decision system that directly or indirectly identify a person on a protected basis, unless made under a permissible defence.
Applies_To: California employers regularly employing 5 or more people, including employers using automated-decision systems in employment decisions; the State and political subdivisions regardless of size; non-profit religious organisations excluded
Notes: Employer duty. Where a vendor's system performs the recruitment or inquiry on the employer's behalf, the agent-as-employer rule (section 11008(b), (f)(3)) can reach the agent — see CA-FEHA-11008.

Plain_Summary: Online application technology that limits, screens out, ranks or prioritises applicants by schedule availability is unlawful under section 11016(c)(3)(A) unless the screening is job-related and consistent with business necessity and the technology includes a mechanism for the applicant to request an accommodation.
Theme: Pre-employment practices — schedule screening and accommodation mechanism
Applies_To: California employers regularly employing 5 or more people, including employers using automated-decision systems in employment decisions; the State and political subdivisions regardless of size; non-profit religious organisations excluded
Notes: Both conditions must hold: job-related and business-necessary screening, and an accommodation-request mechanism built into the tool.

Plain_Summary: Where an automated-decision system measures skill, dexterity, reaction time or other abilities (section 11016(c)(5)), or analyses tone of voice, facial expressions or other physical characteristics (section 11016(d)(1)), it may disadvantage people on the basis of disability, race, national origin, gender or other protected bases, so reasonable accommodation may be needed under Articles 8 and 9 of the regulations.
Theme: Pre-employment practices — accommodation for ADS assessments
Applies_To: California employers regularly employing 5 or more people, including employers using automated-decision systems in employment decisions; the State and political subdivisions regardless of size; non-profit religious organisations excluded
Notes: Accommodation duty sits with the employer. The vendor's tool design determines whether accommodation is practically possible, but the regulations place no freestanding duty on the vendor.

Plain_Summary: Section 11017(a) makes a policy or practice with adverse impact on a protected basis unlawful unless it is job-related and consistent with business necessity, and adopts the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures (29 C.F.R. 1607 (1978)). Section 11017(e) applies the same test to a facially neutral testing device, automated-decision system or other selection means with adverse impact: it is permissible only on a showing that it is job-related and consistent with business necessity.
Theme: Employee selection — adverse impact and business necessity
Applies_To: California employers regularly employing 5 or more people, including employers using automated-decision systems in employment decisions; the State and political subdivisions regardless of size; non-profit religious organisations excluded
Notes: The business-necessity showing is a defence burden that arises when adverse impact exists, not a freestanding duty to run an impact assessment. Federal disparate-impact enforcement policy (EO 14281) does not pre-empt this state framework.

Plain_Summary: Section 11017.1(a)(1) prohibits inquiring about criminal history through an employment application, background check, internet search or automated-decision system before a conditional offer of employment, subject to the exemptions in section 11017.1(a)(4).
Applies_To: California employers regularly employing 5 or more people, including employers using automated-decision systems in employment decisions; the State and political subdivisions regardless of size; non-profit religious organisations excluded
Notes: Automated-decision-system-specific prohibition; the section 11017.1(a)(4) exemptions are not detailed in this row.

Plain_Summary: Section 11072, item (F), states that the use of an automated-decision system, in the absence of additional process or actions, does not constitute an individualized assessment for disability selection purposes; alternate tests or individualized assessments are the recognised alternative.
Applies_To: California employers regularly employing 5 or more people, including employers using automated-decision systems in employment decisions; the State and political subdivisions regardless of size; non-profit religious organisations excluded
Notes: Corrected citation: Pass 0 attributed this sentence to section 11071(f); the official Final Text places it in section 11072, item (F). The parent subdivision letter is verified: §11072(b)(5), item (F), read in the official CRD Final Text 21 Nov 2026 (FEHA-U2 closed in Fix Pass 1; closure re-confirmed in Fix Pass 2, 21 Nov 2026). Section 11071(e) is the separate provision on medical or psychological examinations administered through an automated-decision system.

Plain_Summary: An employer must not use an automated decision system in three prohibited ways: to breach or prevent compliance with federal, state or local labor, occupational health and safety, employment or civil-rights law; to infer an employee's protected status; or to predict and act adversely against a worker for exercising legal rights. An employer must not rely solely on such a system for a discipline or termination decision; where reliance is primary, a human must corroborate the output using the data behind it or other supporting information, and output that cannot be corroborated or is found inaccurate, incomplete or misleading must not be used. An employee may request, and the employer must provide, a meaningful objective description of the employee's own data used by the system, with other persons' personal information anonymized.
Theme: Human corroboration and prohibited ADS uses
Applies_To: All employers using an ADS: the three prohibited uses in §1522(a) apply to any ADS use; the sole-reliance ban, corroboration, non-use and data-description duties apply where an ADS is used for a discipline or termination decision, with corroboration and the data description triggered by primary reliance
Notes: Ch. 859, Stats. 2026; approved 30 Sep 2026; operative 1 Jul 2027 (§1526.7). Duties fall on the employer only; the statute imposes no duty on the ADS vendor or provider. No small-employer exemption and no size threshold. The part does not apply where a collective bargaining agreement explicitly waives it in clear and unambiguous terms and meets the §1526.5 conditions, or to ADS use covered by the federal aircraft / national-security carve-out in §1526.6. The statute does not define primarily relies; no Labor Commissioner guidance or case law yet as of 2026-11-21.

Plain_Summary: An employer that primarily relied on an automated decision system for a discipline or termination decision must give the affected employee a written post-use notice at the time the decision is communicated. The notice must be in plain language, sent as a separate stand-alone communication, in the language used for routine employee communications, and delivered by a simple easy-to-use method such as email, a hyperlink or another written format. It must state that the employer primarily relied on the system, that a human reviewed and corroborated the decision, how to contact a human for more information about the decision and about the right to a description of the employee's own data, and that retaliation for exercising rights under the part is prohibited.
Applies_To: Employers primarily relying on an ADS for a discipline or termination decision
Notes: Ch. 859, Stats. 2026; operative 1 Jul 2027 (§1526.7). The retaliation prohibition stated in the notice is a content item here; the substantive anti-retaliation duty is §1526 (see CA-SB947-1526). Scope conditions in §1526.5 (collective bargaining agreement waiver) and §1526.6 (federal aircraft / national-security carve-out) apply to the part as a whole.

Plain_Summary: An employer must not discharge, threaten to discharge, demote, suspend, or in any other way discriminate or retaliate against an employee for using or attempting to use rights under this part, filing a complaint with the Labor Commissioner, alleging a violation, cooperating with an investigation or prosecution, or otherwise invoking or assisting enforcement of the part.
Applies_To: Employers covered by Lab. Code Part 5.5.5, in relation to employees exercising rights under the part
Notes: Ch. 859, Stats. 2026; operative 1 Jul 2027 (§1526.7). Enforcement: Labor Commissioner (§1526.1(a)) and public prosecutors (§1526.1(b)); civil penalty of $500 per violation (§1526.1(e)). ATTORNEY FLAG: §1526.1(c) says deactivation where the rest of the part says termination — the word deactivation appears nowhere else in the part; do not paraphrase it away. Scope conditions in §1526.5 (collective bargaining agreement waiver) and §1526.6 (federal aircraft / national-security carve-out) apply to the part as a whole.

Plain_Summary: A voluntary designation framework for independent verification organisations that assess AI systems for compliance with state law. The Government Operations Agency must publish application requirements, procedures and designation criteria on or before 1 Jan 2028, consult stakeholders and convene working groups that report to the Legislature, and receive an annual report from each designated organisation; a conforming audit is relevant but not conclusive evidence in a harm action.
Applies_To: Government Operations Agency (designation and oversight duties); independent verification organisations as the designated class; no duty on an organisation unless it voluntarily engages a designated organisation
Notes: No organisation is required to engage a designated organisation or undergo a covered AI audit. The chapter also states there is no liability solely for non-compliance with a chapter standard, no state endorsement, and no duty on a designated organisation to conduct compliance audits in order to register. Executive Order N-9-26 targets completion of the designation criteria by 1 May 2027.

Plain_Summary: The Government Operations Agency must establish an AI Auditor Registry on its website by 1 Jan 2029, fix annual registration fees, and open a misconduct-reporting mechanism; from 1 Jan 2029 no person may offer, sell, or conduct a covered AI audit unless registered. Registered auditors must file registration information including a standard operating procedure referencing the standards applied, update it within 90 days of a material change, audit to widely recognised standards, report to the auditee, retain records for at least 10 years, meet independence standards, and protect whistleblowers; the agency may investigate, remove a registrant, and refer violations onward.
Applies_To: Government Operations Agency (registry duties); AI auditors offering covered AI audits in California (registration bar from 1 Jan 2029); no direct duty on an organisation unless it engages an auditor for a covered AI audit
Notes: Registration numbers must be shown on advertising offering covered AI audit services (§11549.83.5). Audits required under other laws in force before these chapters took effect are unaffected (§11549.86(a)). No penalty amount and no private right of action are stated in the chapter. Executive Order N-9-26 targets completion of the registry work by 1 Dec 2027. The November 2026 Government Operations Agency report recommending mandatory verification oversight is a proposal, not law.
